title: Granular monetary policy surprises
summary: Falko Fecht, Björn Imbierowicz and Moritz Kellers find that a common ECB announcement can generate different policy repricing across the banks that lend to the same firm. Those differences show up most clearly in new short-term loans to small businesses. Across the distance between the tenth and ninetieth percentiles of the bank-specific surprise, their estimated small-firm pricing difference is 22–38 basis points over the first two complete months after the meeting. The corresponding response for large firms is close to zero. A single market-wide event measure would hide that difference, even if it measured the aggregate surprise accurately.

The authors combine regulatory money-market and derivatives transactions covering 36 Governing Council meetings from January 2021 to June 2025. For an overnight index swap executed before the announcement, they compare the bank’s actual fixed rate with the volume-weighted post-conference rate across banks for the same event, maturity band and direction of trade. Comparing a pay-fixed trade with similar trades helps avoid mechanically manufacturing a surprise from the bid–ask spread. An alternative benchmark excludes the bank’s own transactions. The aggregate series tracks conventional euro-area surprises, yet within-event differences across banks are of a similar order to variation in the aggregate series across dates. An executed swap price reflects hedging needs, inventory, client flows and timing as well as expectations. The measure does not reveal each bank’s private forecast of the policy rate.

The loan exercise compares different lenders to the same borrower in the same month. A fixed effect for each firm-month absorbs common policy news and borrower-specific conditions shared across lenders, including much of the demand for credit. The analysis concerns newly originated euro-denominated, fixed-rate short-term credit with maturity of up to one year. Controlling for loan amount, instrument type and maturity leaves the early size difference largely intact. Both upward and downward surprises transmit to small-firm rates, supporting a reading in which a borrower’s relationship shapes which lender assessment enters the price. The evidence does not establish that the same repricing applies to longer loans, outstanding credit stocks or firms with a single banking relationship.

Two separate exercises show why a lender’s loan-setting response should be distinguished from its other exposures. A ten-basis-point absolute surprise is associated with approximately €1 million lower proprietary equity-trading profit in the interval ending on the meeting day. The authors trace this association to the common event intensity among banks active in swaps. In the corporate overnight deposit sample, a ten-basis-point surprise is associated with about 11–12 basis points of cumulative rate repricing after five to ten business days. The common policy component has a detectable effect on deposits, while the bank-relative effect is imprecise. The combination provides little support for interpreting every small-firm loan difference as a simple pass-through of that bank’s observed deposit-price change.

The paper also compares monetary-policy speeches with Governing Council decisions. Bank-relative pricing changes around the measured speeches do not produce an analogous, precisely estimated lending pattern when the two event classes enter together. Limited trading in short event windows constrains the comparison. Overall, the result concerns the distribution of prices at which credit reaches borrowers and the particular markets in which common or bank-specific news appears. The authors do not infer that a higher quoted loan rate necessarily reduced the firm’s total borrowing or investment.

questions.question: Does the within-borrower rate difference also change the total credit a small business can obtain?
questions.detail: The study identifies prices on newly originated short-maturity credit for firms observed with multiple lenders. Multi-lender firms may shift borrowing when one lender reprices. Compare bank offers, drawdowns, total firm borrowing and credit-line utilisation in credit-register data. The answer determines whether the result represents costly aggregate tightening or a redistribution of lending relationships.

questions.question: Which features of a bank’s swap activity predict persistent lending differences?
questions.detail: The measure captures executed prices, including inventory and hedging as well as expectations. Compare maturities, client-facing flows, pre-existing risk exposures and transaction timing against subsequent loan pricing in supervisory records. A repeatable exposure would matter for assessing bank margins and SME funding risk; idiosyncratic execution noise would be much less useful.

questions.question: Does the distinction between common deposit repricing and lender-specific loan pricing persist in other funding regimes?
questions.detail: The sample spans 36 meetings and covers active corporate overnight deposits, with limited information about depositors. Seek evidence across alternative cycles, retail deposits and banks with different funding structures using matched supervisory datasets. This would clarify how far net interest margin assumptions can be extrapolated across institutions or maturities. Check whether credit-line funding follows the same pattern.
